entries.title: Technique: Hermitization (Girko's Method) for Non-Hermitian Random Matrices
entries.statement: TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To study the empirical spectral distribution of a non-Hermitian random matrix M, such as an i.i.d.-entry matrix in the circular law problem, Girko's Hermitization method associates to each z in C the 2n x 2n Hermitian matrix H_z with off-diagonal blocks M-zI and (M-zI)^*, whose eigenvalues are plus and minus the singular values of M-zI. The identity log|det(M-zI)| = (1/2) sum_i log(s_i(M-zI)^2) relates the real part of the logarithmic potential of M's empirical spectral distribution at z to the empirical distribution of singular values of M-zI, a Hermitian and hence more tractable object accessible via Stieltjes transform and local law techniques from Hermitian random matrix theory. Establishing, first, convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI for almost every z, and second, a uniform bound preventing accumulation of small singular values near 0, needed because log is singular there, together imply, via potential-theoretic uniqueness, convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of M itself, for example to the circular law for i.i.d. entries. It does not work without the delicate small-singular-value control, typically the hardest and most technical part of the proof, requiring separate anti-concentration or least-singular-value estimates, and the method inherently gives information about the logarithmic potential, from which the actual distribution is recovered only via a separate potential-theoretic uniqueness argument. Typical failure: Establishing convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI and concluding convergence of the eigenvalue distribution of M without separately proving the required small-singular-value control; without a quantitative lower bound on the least singular value, which can be genuinely delicate for matrices with dependent or heavy-tailed entries, the logarithmic potential argument can fail even though the easier half of Girko's method has been verified, historically the main obstruction in proving circular-law universality under weak entry assumptions. entries.title: Technique: Poisson-Dirichlet Limits and the Durrett-Liggett Smoothing Transform
entries.statement: TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.
assumptions: for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory
for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied
independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation
non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution

entries.title: Technique: Schur Complement Identity for Determinantal Conditional Kernels
entries.statement: TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a determinantal point process with correlation kernel K, Hermitian and satisfying 0<=K<=I in the discrete finite-space setting, the conditional law of the process restricted to a subset given the exact configuration on the complementary subset is again determinantal, with a kernel given by a Schur-complement formula. Partitioning the index set into A, the observed subset, and B, the remaining subset, and writing K in block form with entries K_AA, K_AB, K_BA, K_BB, the conditional kernel on B given the exact points observed in A is expressed via a Schur-complement expression such as K_BB - K_BA (K_AA - I)^{-1} K_AB, with the precise form depending on the convention used (correlation kernel versus L-ensemble) and on whether one conditions on points being present or absent in A. This identity is the fundamental tool for analyzing conditioning, dynamics, and Gibbs-type properties of determinantal processes, including eigenvalues of random matrices, non-intersecting paths, discrete orthogonal polynomial ensembles, and, via the transfer-current theorem, uniform spanning trees, reducing conditional analysis to linear algebra on the kernel matrix. It does not apply outside the determinantal class of point processes, or its Pfaffian analogue for orthogonal and symplectic ensembles, which has a related but distinct formula, and the exact form of the Schur complement depends sensitively on the specific conditioning event and on invertibility of the relevant block, which can fail or require a pseudo-inverse or limiting argument at special parameter values. Typical failure: Applying a Schur-complement conditional-kernel formula derived under one convention, such as conditioning an L-ensemble on a fixed exact sample, to a different conditioning question, such as conditioning on a sub-event like at least one point in a region, or mixing up the correlation-kernel and L-ensemble conventions, without re-deriving the correct formula; determinantal-process conditioning identities are convention-sensitive, and mixing them up produces a kernel that still looks plausible, expressed via some Schur complement, but does not correctly describe the actual conditional process. Canonical reference: Shirai and Takahashi, 2003, Journal of Functional Analysis; Borodin and Rains, 2005, Journal of Statistical Physics; Lyons, 2003, Annals of Probability.
assumptions: the point process is exactly determinantal, or Pfaffian with the analogous but distinct formula, with a well-defined correlation kernel K satisfying the standard positivity and boundedness conditions
the conditioning event is of the specific form covered by the Schur-complement formula, i.e. an exact configuration on a subset, or the corresponding L-ensemble conditioning
invertibility, or a well-defined limiting or pseudo-inverse procedure, for the relevant diagonal block appearing in the formula, e.g. K_AA - I
the block partition A, B is taken with respect to the same index set on which K is originally defined
